title: Why doubling substrate stops doubling speed

scenes.tts: Why can doubling an enzyme's substrate produce far less than double the product? Watch this enzyme make forty-five micromoles per minute at twelve millimolar substrate. What happens at twenty-four?
scenes.caption: Why can doubling an enzyme's substrate produce far less than double the product? Watch this enzyme make 45 micromoles per minute at 12 mM substrate. What happens at 24 mM?
scenes.visual: Fill the frame with a large schematic enzyme assay: four blue enzyme booths cycle between EMPTY and BUSY while yellow substrate discs drift continuously from left to right. A computed readout above them settles at '[S] = 12 mM' and 'v = 45 micromoles/min'. During the final question, a slider moves from 12 to 24 mM, the substrate stream doubles, and the velocity readout becomes a pulsing question mark. Keep discs flowing and booths cycling throughout. No molecular structures.
scenes.narration: Why can doubling an enzyme's substrate produce far less than double the product? Watch this enzyme make 45 micromoles per minute at 12 mM substrate. What happens at 24 mM?

scenes.visual: Hold the question 'At 24 mM: 90 micromoles/min?' in large high-contrast text above the same moving assay. The doubled yellow substrate stream continues drifting; blue booths keep processing at their existing cadence; the velocity question mark gently pulses. This is the deliberate thinking pause.

Transform the pulsing question into the title 'Why doubling substrate stops doubling speed' for two seconds. Keep the assay visible behind it at reduced brightness, with substrate discs and booth gates still moving.

scenes.tts: In its simplest form, picture each enzyme as a toll booth with no waiting lane. A substrate car enters only an empty booth. A busy booth converts that car to product, then opens again.
scenes.visual: Brighten and enlarge the four carried booths into a toll plaza occupying most of the frame. Yellow substrate discs smoothly transform into small yellow cars labelled 'S'; each enters an open blue booth labelled 'E', changes inside into a green car labelled 'P', and exits right. A car reaching a closed BUSY gate curves away along a return loop instead of queuing. Stagger the four booth cycles so gates and cars move continuously. Label the whole picture 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: In its simplest form, picture each enzyme as a toll booth with no waiting lane. A substrate car enters only an empty booth. A busy booth converts that car to product, then opens again.

scenes.tts: With little substrate, most booths stand empty. Nearly every extra car finds one, so adding substrate almost proportionally increases product flow. The limiting factor is arrivals, not the booths' working speed.
scenes.visual: Use the same plaza at low traffic. Keep three or four gates visibly open while sparse yellow cars arrive. A small 'substrate in' counter and green 'product out' counter both climb together at nearly matching rates. As 'adding substrate' is spoken, increase arrivals modestly and make the product counter accelerate proportionally; the internal booth-cycle animation keeps the same speed.
scenes.narration: With little substrate, most booths stand empty. Nearly every extra car finds one, so adding substrate almost proportionally increases product flow. The limiting factor is arrivals, not the booths' working speed.

scenes.tts: Add more substrate, and empty booths become scarce. Cars finding busy booths drive on and try again later. Product still flows, but each added car buys less extra speed.
scenes.visual: Continuously thicken the yellow traffic stream through the same plaza. More gates flip from EMPTY to BUSY, and rejected cars peel smoothly into the return loop. The green product counter continues rising, but its acceleration visibly tapers while the yellow arrival counter accelerates. A vertical 'busy fraction' gauge rises toward full without reaching it.
scenes.narration: Add more substrate, and empty booths become scarce. Cars finding busy booths drive on and try again later. Product still flows, but each added car buys less extra speed.

scenes.tts: Here is the guiding idea. Velocity equals k cat, one busy enzyme's turnover pace, times the amount of busy enzyme. Substrate changes the busy amount, but it cannot make each busy enzyme work faster.
scenes.caption: Here is the guiding idea. Velocity equals kcat, one busy enzyme's turnover pace, times the amount of busy enzyme. Substrate changes the busy amount, but it cannot make each busy enzyme work faster.
scenes.visual: Keep the moving plaza on the left and build a large relationship on the right from its parts: 'velocity' beside the live product counter, then '= kcat x busy enzyme'. Highlight one booth and show its gate completing identical timed cycles under a steady kcat metronome. Increase yellow arrivals so the number of BUSY booths rises, while the highlighted booth's cycle rate remains unchanged.
scenes.narration: Here is the guiding idea. Velocity equals kcat, one busy enzyme's turnover pace, times the amount of busy enzyme. Substrate changes the busy amount, but it cannot make each busy enzyme work faster.

scenes.tts: Now transform the toll plaza into a graph. Substrate concentration runs across the bottom; initial velocity climbs upward. The moving car counter becomes points on the Michaelis-Menten curve, computed from the equation.
scenes.visual: Shrink the carried plaza into the lower-left corner, then transform its yellow arrival counter into the x-axis '[S]' and its green product counter into the y-axis 'initial velocity'. Sweep substrate from low to high; for each value, plot the computed point from v = 60[S]/(4 + [S]). Join the points into a smooth blue hyperbola while a small booth icon travels along it. Label the graph 'computed', not schematic.
scenes.narration: Now transform the toll plaza into a graph. Substrate concentration runs across the bottom; initial velocity climbs upward. The moving car counter becomes points on the Michaelis-Menten curve, computed from the equation.

scenes.tts: Velocity equals V max times substrate concentration, divided by K m plus substrate concentration. The fraction is the share of enzyme that is busy. As that share approaches one, velocity approaches V max.
scenes.caption: Velocity equals Vmax times substrate concentration, divided by Km plus substrate concentration. The fraction is the share of enzyme that is busy. As that share approaches one, velocity approaches Vmax.
scenes.visual: Keep the computed curve moving with the booth icon. Build the text equation 'v = Vmax x [S] / (Km + [S])' above it, one term transforming from the counters already on screen. Beside the fraction, reuse the four-booth row: animate one, then two, then nearly all four booths becoming BUSY as [S] rises. A blue Vmax ceiling line extends across the graph as the curve approaches it.
scenes.narration: Velocity equals Vmax times substrate concentration, divided by Km plus substrate concentration. The fraction is the share of enzyme that is busy. As that share approaches one, velocity approaches Vmax.

scenes.tts: K m marks the substrate concentration where that busy fraction is one half. Therefore, velocity is half of V max there. K m is a half-speed point, not automatically a measure of binding affinity.
scenes.caption: Km marks the substrate concentration where that busy fraction is one half. Therefore, velocity is half of Vmax there. Km is a half-speed point, not automatically a measure of binding affinity.
scenes.visual: Move the booth icon to [S] = 4 mM on the computed curve. Exactly two of the four carried booths become BUSY. Draw a dashed horizontal line from 30 micromoles/min to the curve and a dashed vertical line down to 'Km = 4 mM'; bracket 30 as 'one half Vmax'. Then replace a tempting label 'affinity' with a small crossed-out tag while 'half-speed point' remains bright.
scenes.narration: Km marks the substrate concentration where that busy fraction is one half. Therefore, velocity is half of Vmax there. Km is a half-speed point, not automatically a measure of binding affinity.

scenes.tts: V max is the speed approached when nearly every enzyme is busy. It equals k cat times total enzyme concentration. More substrate cannot raise that ceiling, but adding enzyme can.
scenes.caption: Vmax is the speed approached when nearly every enzyme is busy. It equals kcat times total enzyme concentration. More substrate cannot raise that ceiling, but adding enzyme can.
scenes.visual: Sweep the booth icon toward high [S] as three, then nearly all four booths remain BUSY and the curve hugs the Vmax = 60 ceiling. Pour in more yellow cars; the same ceiling holds and rejected cars loop away. Then transform the booth row into a blue 'enzyme amount' gauge rising from one-fold to two-fold and smoothly lift the computed ceiling and curve to Vmax = 120, with Km still 4 mM (half-speed now 60).
scenes.narration: Vmax is the speed approached when nearly every enzyme is busy. It equals kcat times total enzyme concentration. More substrate cannot raise that ceiling, but adding enzyme can.

scenes.tts: Return to our enzyme: V max is sixty micromoles per minute, and K m is four millimolar. At twelve millimolar, three quarters are busy, giving forty-five. At twenty-four, about six sevenths are busy, giving roughly fifty-one.
scenes.caption: Return to our enzyme: Vmax is 60 micromoles per minute, and Km is 4 mM. At 12 mM, three quarters are busy, giving 45. At 24 mM, about six sevenths are busy, giving roughly 51.
scenes.visual: Restore the original four-booth row and computed curve with Vmax = 60 and Km = 4. Animate a marker from [S] = 12 to [S] = 24. At 12, three of four booths are BUSY beside 'v = 45'; transform that display at 24 into a 6/7 busy gauge and 'v approximately 51'. A live substitution strip below updates from '60 x 12/(4+12)' to '60 x 24/(4+24)'.
scenes.narration: Return to our enzyme: Vmax is 60 micromoles per minute, and Km is 4 mM. At 12 mM, three quarters are busy, giving 45. At 24 mM, about six sevenths are busy, giving roughly 51.

scenes.tts: Doubling substrate raised velocity only about fourteen percent, because just one quarter of the enzyme was empty initially. Far below K m, doubling substrate nearly doubles velocity. Near saturation, it barely helps.
scenes.caption: Doubling substrate raised velocity only about 14 percent, because just one quarter of the enzyme was empty initially. Far below Km, doubling substrate nearly doubles velocity. Near saturation, it barely helps.
scenes.visual: Keep the computed curve and slide a translucent doubling bracket across it. At low [S], for example 0.2 to 0.4 mM (computed v 2.9 to 5.5), show the paired points nearly doubling in height. Move the same bracket to 12 and 24 mM; the height changes only from 45 to about 51, and a green '+14%' label grows between them. The busy-fraction gauge rises only from 3/4 to about 6/7.
scenes.narration: Doubling substrate raised velocity only about 14 percent, because just one quarter of the enzyme was empty initially. Far below Km, doubling substrate nearly doubles velocity. Near saturation, it barely helps.

scenes.tts: So ask how much enzyme is still empty before predicting a substrate effect. The curve bends because the busy fraction approaches one, not because catalysis stops. More substrate adds speed only by filling empty enzymes.
scenes.visual: Transform the graph back into the carried toll plaza. A large EMPTY share shrinks as traffic increases while BUSY booths continue cycling and green product cars keep exiting. Place the question 'How much enzyme is still empty?' above the plaza; then let the line 'More substrate adds speed only by filling empty enzymes' settle beneath the continuously working booths.
scenes.narration: So ask how much enzyme is still empty before predicting a substrate effect. The curve bends because the busy fraction approaches one, not because catalysis stops. More substrate adds speed only by filling empty enzymes.

scenes.visual: End card over the still-moving plaza: 'More substrate adds speed only by filling empty enzymes.' Keep booth gates cycling and a few product cars exiting beneath the line for all three seconds.
